passage:
Study chat, Tuesday night.
Harish: Rank list is up. Payal, you're third. Neel, ninth.
Neel: Payal, can you send the geometry notes you made?
Payal: I'll look for them tomorrow.
Harish: You found them in two minutes last term. I saw you tuck the notebook under your bag when Neel walked by 😅
Payal: Everyone's counting everyone's marks now. Whoever tops gets called up on stage.
Neel: Remember the science model? We swapped every single note for that. 🙂
Harish: Nobody hid anything, and we finished in three days.
Payal: ...okay. Give me till morning.

qa.q: What did Harish see Payal do when Neel walked by?
qa.a: Harish saw Payal tuck the notebook under the bag when Neel walked by.

qa.q: What might Harish be feeling when pointing out the notebook tucked under the bag?
qa.a: Harish seems a little frustrated by the hiding but keeps the tone light, wanting the easy sharing of the science model back.

qa.q: What could Harish or Neel do to bring back the sharing they had during the science model?
qa.a: They could suggest studying in a small group, as they did for the model, and offer their own notes first.

qa.q: What might it be like for Payal, who used to share notes, to be asked for them now?
qa.a: Payal may feel pulled between friendship and the rank list, which fits the late answer, “Give me till morning.”

grounding: An observer notices that a class ranking makes people guard their notes, while group work had them sharing everything.

passage: Irfan noticed it first in mock-exam week. The rank list hung outside the staffroom, and by lunch Alka had started shielding her notebook with her arm when anyone came near. Last term she had passed her chemistry notes down the whole bench. Now when Zubair asked, she said, “Left them at home.” Two weeks earlier, building a rainwater-tank model for the science fair, six of them had shared everything under the mango tree: pencils, ideas, even lunch. Irfan watched the group leave the notice board in twos and threes, saying nothing about ranks. Alka caught Irfan's eye, closed the notebook, and then, slowly, opened it again and slid it toward Zubair.

qa.q: Where did the six share pencils, ideas and lunch while building the rainwater-tank model?
qa.a: They shared them under the mango tree.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling while watching the group leave the notice board in silence?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt uneasy and a little sad, missing the easy sharing under the mango tree that the rank list had pushed aside.

qa.q: What could a teacher do so that classmates keep sharing notes in exam week?
qa.a: A teacher could give some group tasks or share-and-explain sessions and avoid posting a rank list, so that helping each other is rewarded.

qa.q: What might Alka have felt when she caught Irfan's eye and then slid the notebook toward Zubair?
qa.a: Alka may have felt a little caught out or ashamed, and then relieved to do what she used to do.

grounding: A student sees that a class ranking makes people hide their notes while the group project had them sharing.

passage: At the international school in Singapore, the chemistry teacher posted a ranking after every test, names in order from first to twenty-eighth. Noa watched it change her class. Mei, who used to photocopy her notes for anyone, now kept her folder zipped inside her bag. Two friends who had shared lunch since Year 7 stopped sitting together after one of them overtook the other by a single mark. Then, in March, a different teacher set a group lab project with one shared grade. Noa noticed Mei unzip the folder again. Dev, who had been near the bottom of the list, explained the titration so clearly that the whole group clapped. Noa wondered which version of her classmates was the real one.

qa.q: What did the chemistry teacher post after every test?
qa.a: A ranking, names in order from first to twenty-eighth.

qa.q: What does Noa's wondering at the end suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Noa seems puzzled and uneasy, troubled by how much the ranking changed her classmates' behaviour.

qa.q: What could the chemistry teacher change, based on what Noa saw?
qa.a: Drop the public ranking and use more shared-grade group work, so classmates have a reason to help each other.

qa.q: How might the ranking feel for Mei?
qa.a: Mei likely felt pressured and guarded, hiding notes she once shared freely, and was relieved to share again once the grade was shared.

grounding: A student notices a class ranking turning friends into rivals, while group work with a shared grade brings back mutual help.

passage: In the evening study hall of the coaching centre in Kota, the weekly rank list was pinned beside the water cooler. Bhavna noticed how people walked past it: quickly, eyes down, then back for a second look. Francis, ranked fourth, used to explain physics doubts to anyone who asked. This week, when Imtiaz asked him about lenses, Francis said, 'Figure it out, yaar,' and put on his headphones. Imtiaz was ranked fifth. At the next table, though, the students from the Sunday study circle, who didn't care much about ranks, were drawing ray diagrams together on one sheet, arguing and laughing. Bhavna looked at her own notes, tucked under her arm, and slowly slid them onto the table between her and her roommate.

qa.q: Where was the weekly rank list pinned?
qa.a: Beside the water cooler in the study hall.

qa.q: What does Bhavna sliding her notes onto the table suggest?
qa.a: Bhavna seems moved by the study circle's warmth and a little uncomfortable with her own guardedness, so she chooses to share.

qa.q: What could the centre try to reduce the rivalry Bhavna saw?
qa.a: Stop pinning ranks publicly and set up more study circles where students solve problems together.

qa.q: Why might Francis have refused Imtiaz this week?
qa.a: Francis may have felt threatened, since Imtiaz was ranked just below at fifth, and helping felt like giving away an edge.

grounding: A student sees a public rank list make classmates hide help, while a cooperative study circle shares freely.

passage:
Dear Lakshmi ma'am,
You always said a class is like a family. My new school isn't like that. Here, every Monday the class teacher reads out the top ten, and the top ten get to sit in the front row. I've noticed that people stopped lending notes after the first reading. When Sanjana was absent with a fever, nobody sent her the maths notes, and she came back two chapters behind. I sent mine late at night, and I felt like I was doing something secret.
But in art period, where we paint group murals, it's completely different. Everyone lends brushes, and Farhan helped Sanjana with her shading for twenty minutes.
It's the same people. I keep thinking about that.
Your student always,
Ishita

qa.q: Who gets to sit in the front row?
qa.a: The top ten, read out every Monday.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel sending the maths notes late at night?
qa.a: Ishita felt uneasy, as if doing something secret, because sharing had become unusual in the class.

qa.q: What might Ishita suggest to the class teacher?
qa.a: Stop reading out the top ten and add group tasks like the murals, so sharing notes feels normal again.

qa.q: What is it like for Sanjana coming back after the fever?
qa.a: She is two chapters behind because nobody sent notes, which likely left her feeling alone and stressed.

grounding: A student notices that ranking makes classmates hide notes, while group murals make the same people help each other.

passage: Ranks? Okay, here's what I saw. I'm Jomon, Class 10, and it happened to my friend Harish. In term one our school pinned a rank list outside the staffroom every month. Harish was number four, Leena number five, me number six. Suddenly Harish stopped lending his physics notes. Leena started studying in the library corner where no one could see her pages. Nobody said anything mean. Everyone just went quiet about what they knew, like knowledge was something you could lose by showing it. In term two a new teacher put us in groups of four with one shared score for projects. First week, Harish was explaining vectors to Leena on the back bench, drawing arrows on her palm with a pen. Same people, same syllabus. Only the rules had changed, and the notes came out of the bags again.

qa.q: What rank was Harish on the term-one list?
qa.a: Harish was number four.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling as classmates went quiet about what they knew?
qa.a: Jomon felt uneasy and a little sad, watching friends turn into guarded rivals even though nobody was being mean.

qa.q: Why did the group projects change how Harish behaved?
qa.a: With one shared score, helping Leena also helped Harish, so explaining vectors made more sense than hiding notes.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt about keeping his physics notes to himself?
qa.a: Harish may have felt pressured and a little guilty, protecting a rank while losing the easy friendship of sharing.

grounding: Jomon observes how a monthly ranking made classmates hide notes while shared-score group work made them help each other.
